journal: Korea Institute of Design Research Society
title: Sound, Symbol, and Space: An Ethnosemiotic Analysis of Vernacular Soundscapes in Honghai Morning Market
setting: street (Honghai Morning Market: ca. 1 km open-air street market in a city in Northeast China, open 05:00-08:00 daily, adjacent to housing and a school)
design: qualitative (ethnosemiotic field study: repeated soundwalks, sound mapping, direct observation, photography, semi-structured interviews)
sample_n: NR (no participant count reported; unit of analysis = market sound events and three stall case studies; 11 customers recorded as attracted at the tofu stall during one 40 min 21 s recording)
exposure: Market soundscape recorded with a ZOOM H6 recorder along a fixed soundwalk route (each walk ca. 40 min, at opening, peak and pre-closure hours) and mapped as 12 representative sources from a 44 min 17 s recording, with decibel values extracted in Adobe Audition (§3-1, §3-2 [page 6-8]). Sounds were coded as performance sounds (dialect hawking calls, food-preparation sounds), navigation sounds (live poultry crowing, water splashing, defeathering machine, weighing scales) and background sounds (conversations, transaction sounds, vehicle honking, wind and bird calls). Reported acoustic features: hawking calls ca. 4 s each with rising intonation and high amplitude; high-decibel chicken crowing at 2000-4000 Hz lasting 1-2 s; defeathering machine ca. 75-85 dB running ca. 4 min per activation; blowtorch hissing at 2000-4000 Hz in 20-30 s bursts with 6-10 s intervals (§4-1 to §4-3 [page 9-12]).
behaviour_measure: Observed immediate behavioural responses to market sounds: bodily orientation adjustments (turning heads, pausing, glancing), spatial movement (approaching the sound source, altering walking paths) and initiation of social interaction (talking to companions or engaging vendors); counts of customers attracted by hawking and of immediate purchases at the tofu stall; vendors' adjustment of hawking frequency and loudness in response to foot traffic and closing time.
measurement_method: observation (direct observation 2-3 visits per week of ca. 1 h each, photography of behavioural reactions, soundwalk field notes; semi-structured interviews are declared in §1-2 and §3-1 but no interview data are reported)
key_finding: Market sounds functioned as a symbolic system that steered users' behaviour: hawking calls, poultry crowing and blowtorch noise triggered acoustic orientation (head turning, pausing), movement towards or away from the source and the start of vendor-customer interaction, and at the tofu stall hawking directly attracted 11 customers of whom 5 bought immediately. In the reverse direction, vendors shaped the soundscape strategically, raising the frequency and volume of hawking during high foot traffic and near closing time (from one call every 9-15 s to one every 3-6 s).
effect_stats: Descriptive counts only; no inferential statistics reported. Tofu stall: 24 hawking calls in 40 min 21 s, every 9-15 s during the first 15 min vs every 3-6 s during the following 25 min; hawking 'directly attracted 11 customers, five of whom made immediate purchases' (§4-1 [page 9-10]). Poultry stall: 48 high-decibel crows totalling ca. 83 s; defeathering machine activated 3 times, ca. 4 min each, ca. 75-85 dB (§4-2 [page 10]). Blowtorch stall: 42 min 17 s recording, bursts of 20-30 s at 6-10 s intervals (§4-3 [page 11]).
